exercises.prompt: Implement applyTwice(f, x) so it returns the result of applying the function f to x twice — that is, f(f(x)). applyTwice(n => n + 1, 5) is 7, because f turns 5 into 6 and then 6 into 7. applyTwice(n => n - 1, 10) is 8. The function f is passed in as an argument, so call it rather than writing the operation yourself.
hints: f is an ordinary function you were handed — call it like any other, f(x), to run it on a value.
You need f applied twice: feed x through once, then feed that result through f again.
return f(f(x)) — the inner f(x) runs first, and its result becomes the argument to the outer f. Applying f only once would return 6, not 7, for n => n + 1 on 5.

exercises.prompt: Implement mapValues(obj, f) so it returns a NEW object with the same keys as obj but each value replaced by f(value). mapValues({a: 1, b: 2}, n => n * 10) is {a: 10, b: 20}. An empty object returns an empty object. Do not modify the input object.
hints: Object.entries(obj) hands you the [key, value] pairs, which you can walk to build a fresh object.
Start from an empty object {}, and for each [k, v] assign out[k] = f(v) — the key is copied unchanged, the value is transformed.
const out = {}; for (const [k, v] of Object.entries(obj)) out[k] = f(v); return out — building a new object leaves the caller's obj untouched, which the last test checks.

exercises.prompt: Implement makeAdder(n) so it returns a NEW function that adds n to whatever it is given. makeAdder is called once to build the adder, then that adder is called with a number: const add5 = makeAdder(5); add5(10) is 15. Two adders built from different n values are independent of each other.

tests.setup:
const a = makeAdder(1)
const b = makeAdder(100)

hints: makeAdder does not add anything itself — it builds and hands back a function that will do the adding later.
Return a one-argument function that remembers n: given x, it produces x + n.
return x => x + n — each call to makeAdder creates a fresh function holding its own n, so add5 and the adder built from 100 never interfere.

exercises.prompt: Implement compose(f, g) so it returns a NEW function that feeds its input through g first and then through f — the result is f(g(x)). const h = compose(x => x + 1, x => x * 2); h(5) is 11, because g doubles 5 to 10 and then f adds 1. Order matters here: g runs before f.

tests.setup: const h = compose(x => x + 1, x => x * 2)
const h = compose(x => x * 2, x => x + 1)
const h = compose(x => x - 3, x => x - 1)
const same = compose(x => x, x => x)

hints: compose returns a function; inside it, you have two functions to run in a specific order on the input.
g is the inner step and f the outer: apply g to x, then apply f to whatever g returned.
return x => f(g(x)) — g runs first. Flipping to g(f(x)) would give 12 instead of 11 for the first test, which is exactly why another test swaps the two functions.

exercises.prompt: Implement countMatching(arr, pred) so it returns how many elements of arr satisfy the predicate function pred — that is, how many elements x make pred(x) return true. countMatching([1, 2, 3, 4, 5], n => n > 2) is 3. An empty array returns 0. pred is supplied by the caller, so apply it rather than hard-coding a test.
hints: pred is a test you can hand to the array methods that expect a callback — you do not write the condition yourself.
filter keeps only the elements that pass pred; the count you want is how many survived.
return arr.filter(pred).length — filter builds the array of matches and .length counts them; returning the filtered array itself, instead of its length, would fail.
